In the figure shown above, we know that 
$m∠A=m∠B.$
What is the measure of the angle $A?$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $x$ be the measure of the interior angle at $A.$ Then,

$$
m∠A=m∠B=x.
$$

*Method 1*

Let's start by finding the value of the missing interior angle at $C.$ We use the fact that the interior and exterior angles are supplementary:

$$
\begin{aligned}{110}^{∘}+m∠C & ={180}^{∘} \\ m∠C & ={180}^{∘}-{110}^{∘} \\ m∠C & ={70}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate $x$ using the fact that the interior angles of a triangle sum to ${180}^{∘}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠A+m∠B+m∠C & ={180}^{∘} \\ x+x+{70}^{∘} & ={180}^{∘} \\ 2x & ={110}^{∘} \\ x & ={55}^{∘}\,\end{aligned}
$$

*Method 2*

We could rewrite the equation $m∠A+m∠B+m∠C={180}^{∘}$ as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{{{180}^{∘}-m∠C}_{⏟}}_{\text{Exterior angle at }C}\,\,\,=m∠A+m∠B.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting, we can solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{{{180}^{∘}-m∠C}_{⏟}}_{\text{Exterior angle at }C}\,\,\, & =m∠A+m∠B \\ {110}^{∘} & =x+x \\ {110}^{∘} & =2x \\ {55}^{∘} & =x\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider a triangle $△ABC$, where the measure of an exterior angle at $C$ is equal to ${127}^{∘}$ and $m∠B={73}^{∘}.$ What is the measure of the angle $A?$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's start by drawing the corresponding triangle.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14191822/assets/0729bbdc2bec04cee7be1f0be31a44648b05a2536f7e17002d1dab6e2f3500c6.png)

*Method 1*

Let's start by finding the value of the missing interior angle at $C.$ We use the fact that the interior and exterior angles are supplementary:

$$
\begin{aligned}{127}^{∘}+m∠C & ={180}^{∘} \\ m∠C & ={180}^{∘}-{127}^{∘} \\ m∠C & ={53}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate $∠A$ using the fact that the interior angles of a triangle sum to ${180}^{∘}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠A+m∠B+m∠C & ={180}^{∘} \\ m∠A+{73}^{∘}+{53}^{∘} & ={180}^{∘} \\ m∠A & ={180}^{∘}-{126}^{∘} \\ m∠A & ={54}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

  

*Method 2*

We could rewrite the equation $m∠A+m∠B+m∠C={180}^{∘}$ as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{{{180}^{∘}-m∠C}_{⏟}}_{\text{Exterior angle at }C}\,\,\,=m∠A+m∠B.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting, we can solve for $m∠A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{{{180}^{∘}-m∠C}_{⏟}}_{\text{Exterior angle at }C}\,\,\, & =m∠A+m∠B \\ {127}^{∘} & =m∠A+{73}^{∘} \\ {127}^{∘}-{73}^{∘} & =m∠A \\ {54}^{∘} & =m∠A\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider a triangle $△ABC$, where an exterior angle at $A$ is ${119}^{∘}$ and an exterior angle at $C$ is ${103}^{∘}.$ What is the measure of the interior angle $B?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's draw a corresponding picture.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14191822/assets/6fc411e7715044257a6818fe63fb3b7bd212c22a2f3d279f282b2b7161be3ecc.png)

   

Let $z$ be the measure of the exterior angle at $B$ pictured above. Since the sum of the exterior angles of a triangle is ${360}^{∘}$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{119}^{∘}+{103}^{∘}+z & ={360}^{∘} \\ {222}^{∘}+z & ={360}^{∘} \\ z & ={138}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can find the value of the missing interior angle at $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠B & ={180}^{∘}-z \\  & ={180}^{∘}-{138}^{∘} \\  & ={42}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $m∠B={42}^{∘}.$

canonical_examples.problem: Given a triangle $\triangle ABC$, let the exterior angles at ${A}$ and ${B}$ be equal $120^\circ$ and $100^\circ,$ respectively. What is the measure of the angle $\angle C?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's start by drawing the corresponding triangle.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14191822/assets/3e2698fe8e2e886127669b1e04f45499706750312b447ff0c73524f2de4ff2ce.png)

  

Let $z$ be the measure of the exterior angle at ${C}$ pictured above. Since the sum of the exterior angles of a triangle is $360^{\circ}$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{120}^{∘}+{100}^{∘}+z & ={360}^{∘} \\ {220}^{∘}+z & ={360}^{∘} \\ z & ={140}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can find the value of the missing interior angle at $C\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠C & ={180}^{∘}-z \\  & ={180}^{∘}-{140}^{∘} \\  & ={40}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $m\angle C = 40^\circ.$

tutorials.name: The Sum of Exterior Angles
tutorials.problem:
Yet another important fact about exterior angles is:

The sum of the measures of the exterior angles of a triangle is always equal to $360^\circ.$

So, for the triangle below, we have 

$$
x+y+z = 360^\circ.
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14191822/assets/22586791e1118a38a554deffaec3ac5b73eafc47eee4be2052c0949dde584cea.png)

To see why, first recall that the measure of an exterior angle is equal to the sum of the measures of the two non-adjacent interior angles. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =m∠B+m∠C \\ y & =m∠A+m∠C \\ z & =m∠A+m∠B.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, remember that the internal angles of a triangle sum to $180^\circ.$ Then we have

$$
\begin{aligned}x+y+z & =(m∠B+m∠C)+(m∠A+m∠C)+(m∠A+m∠B) \\  & =2m∠A+2m∠B+2m∠C \\  & =2(m∠A+m∠B+m∠C) \\  & =2({180}^{∘}) \\  & ={360}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$
